intro.title: PLNJ Simulation
body: You are advising Kathy Ayers, L&N's VP of Marketing and Communications. Plan for about an hour, in addition to reading the case and completing the Canvas steps. You can consult the case at any time.
Round 1 uses the case's numbers. Round 2 and Round 3 include clearly labeled simulation scenarios created for this exercise; those scenarios are not case facts.
The activity does not collect your name, ID, or email. Your decisions and written defense stay in this browser profile on this device.
workflow: Work through three rounds and make your own managerial decisions.
In Rounds 1 and 2, pass both evidence questions to continue. You can retry missed questions as often as needed. Your managerial choices and final defense are unscored.
If you need to stop, reopen the app from Canvas on the same device and browser profile to resume. Start over clears the saved run.
At the end, copy your completion receipt. Return to Canvas, pass the Evidence Check, and submit the Participation Attestation with your receipt. Canvas handles participation credit.

ledger.title: The three budget options
leadIn: Compare the three budget options on projected sales, operating profit, and operating margin. The 7% figure is headquarters' target, not a rule.
The table is a full-year projection. Consumer and trade promotions are treated as independent, and the media reduction is assumed to cost no revenue.
Open the details for spending, calculations, and assumptions. Those projections remain unchanged throughout the simulation.
caseFacts: 2020 forecast: revenue $10,480,000; variable costs $7,336,000; gross profit $3,144,000; wages $920,000; G&A $280,000; marketing $1,400,000; operating profit $544,000 (5.19%).
2020 marketing: paid and owned media $700,000, consumer $400,000, trade $300,000. Media can fall to $500,000 by outsourcing.
Ham's 2018 and 2019 figures are estimates, not observed experiments; no estimate is available for media.
Typical industry revenue-to-cost ratios: 5:1 consumer and 4:1 trade. The plan assumes about 80% capacity. KB Holdings handles reordering, restocking, and delivery.
calculations: Calculation inputs: 2020 revenue was $10,480,000; variable costs were $7,336,000 (70%); gross profit was $3,144,000; wages were $920,000; and G&A was $280,000.
Ham's 2018–2019 sales estimates imply historical average revenue per promotion dollar of 3.65 consumer and 4.65 trade. They are estimates, not observed experiments.
Contribution ROMI = (incremental revenue × 30% − spend) ÷ spend. Consumer: +9.5%; trade: +39.5%; break-even revenue ratio: 3.33.
At industry-typical ratios, the same calculation gives consumer 5:1 → +50% and trade 4:1 → +20%. L&N's consumer ratio is below the industry norm and its trade ratio is above.
The case provides no revenue estimate for paid and owned media. The model reduces media from $700,000 to $500,000 and assumes no sales are lost.
assumptions: Zero revenue loss from the media reduction in all three options. The case says Ham has no media incremental-revenue estimate.
Historical average returns apply to the new or removed promotion dollars (3.65 and 4.65), as if returns were constant at the margin.
Ham's figures are estimates from sales records, expected organic growth, and monthly spend, not observed experiments.
Variable costs stay at 70%; wages ($920K) and G&A ($280K) stay fixed, including at Option 3's implied 87% capacity.
The three levers are independent: consumer and trade revenue are added separately with no interaction. Rounds 2–3 test this.
No promotion calendar change is modeled in Round 1.

rows.label: Profit needed for exactly 7% at that revenue

ledger.note: Option 1 savings: $200,000 paid and owned media + $120,000 consumer + $90,000 trade = $410,000. Cutting promotions alone, without the media cut, gives $497,050 (5.16%). The ledger is the Original projection and is never re-forecast.

round3.considered: Considered in the previous step (not authorized): {label}.
round3.whyOne: You can authorize one adjustment for the rest of the period: retain your plan, refine one execution lever, or redirect the remaining budget. You cannot do two. Your team has three people, and Ryan has said he does not want to split the team's focus. One change at a time also lets you see what moved the results.
round3.commitments: These are already committed and cannot change: your first recommendation ({initialRec}) and confirmed recommendation ({confirmedRec}); your lens ({lens}); the priorities you set ({P}); the calendar you ran ({cal}); the message you used ({msg}); the evidence you watched ({ev}); your response to the Round 2 flag ({response}). The response you considered in the previous step is not listed here: it is not a commitment.
round3.confirmRevisionTitle: This changes your budget direction for the remaining period.
round3.confirmRevision: Money and months already spent are not recovered. The Original projection is not re-forecast.

resultRetain.assumes: the plan, including its gaps, keeps working.
resultRetain.risks: whatever is on your open list.
resultRetain.watch: the measure you chose in Round 2.

resultRefine.assumes: that one lever is the constraint that matters most.
resultRefine.risks: that the other levers stay as they are.
resultRefine.watch: the metric tied to the lever you changed.

resultRevise.assumes: the new direction fits the evidence better than the old one.
resultRevise.risks: that spending moved midyear does not recover past support, and that trade timing changes only at the next trade window.
resultRevise.watch: what the Original projection assumed about the new option.

round3.retainSentence: No change is authorized. The response you considered, "{label}," will not happen.
round3.refineSentence: Only the change you authorized takes effect: your {lever}. The response you considered, "{label}," is not authorized.
round3.reviseSentence: Only the change you authorized takes effect: the remaining budget moves to {option}. The response you considered, "{label}," is not authorized.
round3.noChangeSentence: You considered holding course ("{label}"). You authorized: {action}.
round3.refineCalendar: Changing your calendar takes effect at the next window and applies to the remaining uncommitted media only. A change away from ALIGN returns that media to equal weights; a change to ALIGN shifts it toward the six anchor months from the next window.
round3.refineMessage: Offers already seen by shoppers are not recalled.
round3.refinePriorities: The two you do not choose get no attention for the rest of the period. If you are on an aligned calendar, adding or dropping Awareness continuity changes how the remaining uncommitted media is weighted.

financial.title: Stress-test profit and margin
financial.hint: Use the 70% variable-cost rate: a sales shortfall reduces operating profit by the remaining 30%. For the promotion-return scenario, compare the revised sales estimate with the original and recalculate profit and margin.

variants.prompt: Option 3 projects $11,410,000 in sales and $823,000 in operating profit. Sales come in $120,000 below forecast. Variable costs remain 70% of sales, other costs stay fixed, and Options 1 and 2 are unaffected. Does Option 3 still meet the 7% target and lead on operating profit?

options.label: It meets the 7% target and still leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target and still leads on operating profit.
It meets the 7% target but no longer leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target and no longer leads on operating profit.

variants.explanation: The $120,000 sales shortfall reduces operating profit by 30% × $120,000 = $36,000. Option 3 becomes $787,000 profit on $11,290,000 sales: 6.97%, below 7%. Its $787,000 profit still exceeds Option 2's $763,000 and Option 1's $697,050.

variants.prompt: Option 3 projects $11,410,000 in sales and $823,000 in operating profit. Sales come in $70,000 below forecast. Variable costs remain 70% of sales, other costs stay fixed, and Options 1 and 2 are unaffected. Does Option 3 still meet the 7% target and lead on operating profit?

options.label: It meets the 7% target and still leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target and still leads on operating profit.
It meets the 7% target but no longer leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target and no longer leads on operating profit.

variants.explanation: The $70,000 sales shortfall reduces operating profit by 30% × $70,000 = $21,000. Option 3 becomes $802,000 profit on $11,340,000 sales: 7.07%, above 7%. Its profit remains higher than Options 1 and 2.

variants.prompt: Option 2 projects $11,210,000 in sales and $763,000 in operating profit using an estimated $3.65 in sales per added promotion dollar. In this scenario, each added dollar returns $3.00 instead. With the 70% variable-cost rate and other assumptions unchanged, what does Option 2 project?

options.label: $11.08M sales; $763K profit; 6.89% margin.
$11.21M sales; $763K profit; 6.81% margin.
$11.08M sales; $724K profit; 6.53% margin.
$11.21M sales; $724K profit; 6.46% margin.

variants.explanation: At $3.00 per added dollar, incremental sales are $200,000 × $3.00 = $600,000, which is $130,000 below the $730,000 projection. Profit falls by 30% × $130,000 = $39,000 to $724,000. Sales are $11,080,000, so margin is $724,000 ÷ $11,080,000 = 6.53%.

variants.prompt: Option 1 projects $9,623,500 in sales and $697,050 in operating profit. Sales come in $80,000 below forecast. Variable costs remain 70% of sales, other costs stay fixed, and the other options are unaffected. Does Option 1 still meet the 7% target and lead on operating profit?

options.label: It meets the 7% target and still leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target but still leads on operating profit.
It misses the 7% target and does not lead on operating profit.
It meets the 7% target but does not lead on operating profit.

variants.explanation: The $80,000 sales shortfall reduces operating profit by $24,000. Option 1 becomes $673,050 profit on $9,543,500 sales: about 7.05%, above 7%. Options 2 and 3 remain higher on operating profit.

romi.title: Contribution return on promotion
romi.hint: Revisit the ledger formula: multiply incremental revenue by 30%, subtract promotion spend, then divide by spend.

variants.prompt: A promotion costs $100 and produces $365 in incremental revenue. At a 30% gross margin, what is contribution ROMI?

options.label: The contribution ROMI is 9.5%.
The contribution ROMI is 30.0%.
The contribution ROMI is 39.5%.
The contribution ROMI is 365.0%.

variants.prompt: A promotion costs $100 and produces $465 in incremental revenue. At a 30% gross margin, what is contribution ROMI?

options.label: The contribution ROMI is 9.5%.
The contribution ROMI is 30.0%.
The contribution ROMI is 39.5%.
The contribution ROMI is 465.0%.

variants.prompt: A promotion costs $200 and produces $1,000 in incremental revenue. At a 30% gross margin, what is contribution ROMI?

options.label: The contribution ROMI is 20%.
The contribution ROMI is 30%.
The contribution ROMI is 40%.
The contribution ROMI is 50%.

variants.prompt: A promotion costs $200 and produces $800 in incremental revenue. At a 30% gross margin, what is contribution ROMI?

options.label: The contribution ROMI is 10%.
The contribution ROMI is 20%.
The contribution ROMI is 30%.
The contribution ROMI is 40%.

flow.title: Orders, deliveries, and shopper purchases
flow.hint: Orders are not deliveries, and deliveries are not shopper purchases. With no returns or adjustments, inventory changes by deliveries received minus cases sold.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: in the prior period a retailer sold 100 cases to shoppers. This period it orders 140, receives 120, and sells 100. With no returns or other adjustments, what changed?

options.label: Inventory rises by 20 cases, while shopper purchases stay flat.
Inventory rises by 40 cases, while shopper purchases stay flat.
Inventory falls by 20 cases, while shopper purchases rise.
Inventory stays flat, while shopper purchases rise by 20 cases.

variants.explanation: Deliveries exceed shopper purchases by 20 cases, so inventory rises by 20. Shoppers bought 100 cases in both periods.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: shoppers bought 90 cases last period. This period a retailer orders 155, receives 130, and sells 90. With no returns or other adjustments, what changed?

options.label: Inventory rises by 25 cases, while shopper purchases stay flat.
Inventory falls by 40 cases, while shopper purchases rise.
Inventory stays flat, while shopper purchases fall by 25 cases.
Inventory rises by 40 cases, while shopper purchases stay flat.

variants.explanation: Deliveries exceed shopper purchases by 40 cases, so inventory rises by 40. Shoppers bought 90 cases in both periods.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: shoppers bought 110 cases last period. This period a retailer orders 150, receives 140, and sells 125. With no returns or other adjustments, what changed?

options.label: Inventory stays flat, while shopper purchases fall by 15.
Inventory rises by 25 cases, while shopper purchases rise by 15.
Inventory rises by 15 cases, while shopper purchases rise by 15.
Inventory falls by 15 cases, while shopper purchases stay flat.

variants.explanation: Deliveries exceed shopper purchases by 15 cases, so inventory rises by 15. Shopper purchases rose from 110 to 125.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: shoppers bought 120 cases last period. This period a retailer orders 160, receives 145, and sells 115. With no returns or other adjustments, what changed?

options.label: Inventory rises by 45 cases, while shopper purchases fall by 5.
Inventory rises by 30 cases, while shopper purchases fall by 5.
Inventory falls by 30 cases, while shopper purchases rise by 5.
Inventory stays flat, while shopper purchases stay flat.

variants.explanation: Deliveries exceed shopper purchases by 30 cases, so inventory rises by 30. Shopper purchases fell from 120 to 115.

coordination.title: Retail readiness and promotion timing
coordination.hint: A promotion works at the store only when the offer, display, and available stock are ready together. Revisit the launch timing and store-readiness evidence.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: consumer offers and trade displays are scheduled to start together, but stores receive displays after the offer begins. What should the team do first?

options.label: Keep the offer date and add displays as soon as stores receive them.
Extend the offer at every store, even where displays are delayed.
Confirm displays are in place before launching the offer at those stores.
Move all stores to one launch date, then check display readiness.

variants.explanation: The store launch should wait until the displays are present, with stock available for shoppers.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: L&N can move offer dates. How can the team give shoppers the best chance to see the offer and display together?

options.label: Keep consumer and trade dates separate so stores can prepare each activation.
Coordinate offer and display dates at each store before launch.
Set one shared launch date before confirming each store's readiness.
Move the displays after the consumer offer has already begun.

variants.explanation: Coordinating the offer and display dates before launch gives each store a chance to have both ready when shoppers see the offer.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: consumer and trade promotions will start together in six months. What action best coordinates the launch at participating stores?

options.label: Use one national offer date and let stores adjust displays afterward.
Move the consumer offer ahead of the trade display to build awareness.
Ask stores to move displays after the consumer offer has begun.
Confirm each store's displays and stock before its offer launches.

variants.explanation: Confirm readiness at each participating store before the coordinated offer begins.

variants.prompt: Simulation scenario: shoppers respond to an offer, but several stores report empty shelves. What should the team do before the next offer at those stores?

options.label: Confirm replenishment and displays are ready before the offer launches.
Shift the next offer to another week before checking replenishment.
Keep the next offer date and ask stores to monitor shelf availability.
Use one offer date across stores and review stock after launch.

variants.explanation: Replenishment and displays should be ready before the next offer at the affected stores.
